articles.title: Samuel Stanley Jones: “Prayer is the only source that gives life to our talents”
articles.deck: A Hyderabad worship leader on being chosen to lead, staying undistracted on a stage, and why a gift is never a burden.

hero.alt: Samuel Stanley Jones photographed outdoors by the sea, smiling at the camera

interviewMeta.subject: Samuel Stanley Jones
interviewMeta.subjectBio: A worship leader from Hyderabad. He performed at the 2011 Hyderabad festival with Franklin Graham, and was in the final year of a BTh when this interview was published.

archiveMeta.editNote: First published as Talent Search #1. Lightly edited: the two-column reading order has been repaired, obvious typographical errors corrected, and the questions restored to the order they were asked. The answers are as given.

body.v: On the way to talent search, we found Sam, a young man who discovered his gift as a leader of worship teams. Recently he performed at the Hyderabad festival with Franklin Graham in 2011. A zeal for sharing the gospel led him to study for a BTh, and he is in his final year now.
“I’m doing good by the grace of God”
5Talents: Hi Sam, thanks for the opportunity to conduct an interview with you. How are you doing?
I’m doing good by the grace of God. Thank you.
5Talents: When did you know you wanted to be a worship leader?

Ever since my childhood I’ve been attending regular Sunday school and participated in choir. However, my mother encouraged me in singing and music. Above all this, God has enriched me in leading worship.
5Talents: Did you need special training or coaching, or did it all come naturally?
I believe that it’s a gift from God. To improve this God-given talent, I’ve been attending and participating in the worship ministry.
The next thirty minutes
5Talents: When you get the chance to lead a group of youth in worship, what are your goals right there at that time? What are you hoping you’ll be able to accomplish in the next thirty minutes?

I feel that I’m the source of worship chosen by God to lead the congregation in a holy manner and make them experience the passionate love of God — agape. My goal is to make them feel very easy and comfortable, to make them free from the chains and bondages of the world through the songs I sing, and lead them into worship. I make it very clear to myself that “when God has come to take all our burdens and pains, why should we still carry them?” Keeping this as my agenda, I look forward to the next thirty minutes to make up their minds to easily take the word of God.
5Talents: What does a lifestyle of worship mean to you?

Worship means a lot to me, especially as a worship leader. It simply means to live a life of love. Worship requires something from us, and that is obedience, God-fearing. It is not just a song we sing but a life we live.
It is not just a song we sing but a life we live.
body.attr: On what worship asks of you
body.highlight: not just a song we sing

body.v: 5Talents: What are the things that bring you inspiration as a worship leader personally? I mean, being a leader, we sometimes get distracted by worldly desires. How do you stay inspired?

For me personally, I’m always aware of the process that our hearts take in worship — when my heart begins to soften as the Holy Spirit moves on me, and a desire for God awakens in me. It is a very tough time, especially for the people on the stage facing the audience, to get distracted. I keep myself very cautious of what I’m doing so that shouldn’t be a problem for me.
Sweet wine from the crushed grapes
5Talents: You have discovered the talents in you. Is that so difficult? What do you suggest to those who have not yet discovered their gifts, still unused for the kingdom?

I always get reminded of a quote: “sweet wine from the crushed grapes.” I believe that discovering a talent is never a difficulty or a burden. Talent is an empowering source to our life. Everyone has gifts from God, but we lack knowledge of His will in our lives. I can definitely say that prayer is the only source to give life to our talents, which can be used for the kingdom of God.
5Talents: Being a teen leader, have you experienced others discouraging you? If yes, how do you manage the situation?
Being a teen leader, I don’t say people have discouraged me. In fact there are people who make suggestions to me. I humbly accept them and apply them to my life for my betterment.
5Talents: How would you define your prayer life?

Prayer is the only weapon to overcome anything — that is what I’ve believed since my childhood. We can see things changing only through prayers, and that very much happens in my life too, especially in the time of ministry. Through prayer anything is possible.

articles.title: Mary Sujani has made three hundred puppets, and every one of them preaches
articles.deck: A Hyderabad designer on childhood play that turned into a profession, and on why the smallest talent is worth refining.

hero.alt: Mary Sujani holding two hand puppets, a green bird and an orange one, smiling at the camera

interviewMeta.subject: Mary Sujani
interviewMeta.subjectBio: A designer and curriculum writer working with a Christian organisation in Hyderabad. She has made more than three hundred custom puppets and creative materials for children's ministry.

archiveMeta.editNote: First published as Talent Search #2. Lightly edited: reading order repaired and obvious typographical errors corrected. The answers are as given.

body.v: Introducing Mary Sujani, a multi-talented designer from Hyderabad. She used to play with puppets in childhood, and that interest led her to design and make them. So far she has made more than three hundred custom puppets and creative materials for Christian organisations. The 5Talents team had a nice time interviewing Mary.
5Talents: Hello Mary, greetings from 5Talents. How are you?
I’m fine, thank you.
5Talents: Please share about your professional life.

I’m working with a Christian organisation located in Hyderabad, for more than nine years. My main work is to develop curriculum for children’s Bible schools. Apart from writing Bible lessons for different age groups, I also design illustrations for the children’s workbooks. I’m also deputed for various training programmes at state and all-India level, for training our partners and organisers concerned with our projects, and staff.
5Talents: Please share about the gifts you have received from God.
God gave me skills such as drawing, painting, soft toys, writing skills and making different puppets.
One talent after the other
5Talents: How and when did you discover your talent?
Mmm… at a very young age. Specifically I cannot mention when and how, but I would say that as I was growing up I discovered one talent after the other.
5Talents: Who are your influences?
My family, who also think creatively as I do.
5Talents: Did you need special training or coaching, or did it all come naturally?
It was all natural, but to polish my talents I took vocational courses.
“God showed that He is a refiner”
5Talents: What important lessons has the Lord taught you through your talent?

First of all, I have learnt not to be proud of any of the talents that I received as a gift from God. Secondly, I did not worry about the smallest talent that I had. God showed that He is a refiner, and my life as gold. I walked in faith thinking that God, who kept the seed of talent in me, will surely use me and let it grow in His own time. When I was struggling with my career and I found myself at the crossroads, not knowing what next, the God who saved me placed me in this very ministry and gave me a platform to multiply and use my talents for His glory. I experience success in every step I take.
5Talents: In what ways has God used you to bring blessing to others?
Through my writing and drawing skills many are being blessed and have come to know the Lord. I have seen many transformed stories, and children accepting Christ. I feel so blessed.
5Talents: Have you ever felt inadequate, or not enough? If so, which verse from the Bible helped you to be patient?

Never. God gave me in abundance even before I asked. Based on the life of the farmer in James 5:7–8, I really like these verses for showing the need for patience — because farmers have to be patient. I have also learned the secret of being content in any and every situation, whether well fed or hungry, through Philippians 4:12.
Diamonds people walk over
5Talents: What would you say to someone who is talented but sad, because they are not given an opportunity to use it, or the talent is not recognised by others?

I believe God does not create waste, and never give up. Each individual is valuable. If we walk upon natural diamonds or stones in a wilderness, most of us would ignorantly walk over them and treat them as worthless, having no clue of their value and how beautiful they would look if expertly cut and polished. Likewise, most people might walk over you and never give you an opportunity to shine, or recognise you. Don’t get discouraged. It matters not how people see you. All that matters is the staggering power of God to transform something of breathtaking beauty in you. It is in our hands, friends, whether we want our lives to be a rugged stone or a polished one. Recognise and utilise the opportunities that are placed before you, and leave the rest to God.
Most of us would walk over a diamond in the wilderness and treat it as worthless, having no clue of its value.
5Talents: What would you say to someone who says “I am not very talented — how could God use me?”

It is often used by Christians as an excuse not to do anything to benefit the kingdom of God. They insist on sitting back saying “I am not very talented,” until the Lord finds something for them to excel in. You want to discover what your God-given talents are, and how you should use them for the Lord? Then get busy serving the Lord in some capacity. In doing so, you will find out where your true talents lie, and ultimately where you can best serve the Lord. I did the same, and I encourage you to do the same. Keep in mind, a day is coming when we will all stand before our almighty God, and He will want to know how you have served Him with the talents, time, money and resources entrusted to you. Be a good steward for our Lord Jesus Christ, and ask Him daily how you can serve Him.

articles.title: Every Christian has both natural talents and spiritual gifts
articles.deck: One comes to you at birth and is developed over a life. The other is given by the Spirit for the sake of other people. Knowing which is which changes what you do with them.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published from the July 2012 issue. Reading order repaired, typographical errors corrected, and the prose lightly tightened. The piece carried no byline in the original.

body.v: God created us with a great variety of talents. You may be able to run a marathon, organize a group meeting, teach, or write. Your skill may be typing, photography, or painting. Perhaps you sing or play a musical instrument. Maybe you are a carpenter, landscaper, engineer, mechanic, or bookkeeper. Each of us has a unique function to perform in life and in the Body of Christ.

The Bible refers to the church as the Body of Christ, with Christ as its Head (1 Corinthians 12:27; Ephesians 5:23). Just as your body has many specialised parts, each with its own function, so the church is composed of many individuals — each with his own function to perform, and his own contribution to make, to the rest of the Body.
I encourage you to identify your talents, and ask God to show you how to use them for His glory.
Natural gifts and spiritual gifts

Every Christian possesses both natural talents and spiritual gifts. Our natural abilities come to us at physical birth and are developed through life. Our spiritual gifts are imparted by the Holy Spirit, enabling us to minister to others on behalf of Christ.
Natural gifts
What talents and natural abilities do you have? How did you acquire them, or improve upon them?
According to 1 Corinthians 4:6–7 and Exodus 4:11, what should your attitude be about them? How would you apply Colossians 3:17 to the stewardship of your natural gifts?
Each of you should use whatever gift you have received to serve others, as faithful stewards of God's grace in its various forms. (1 Peter 4:10)

articles.title: He saw a photograph of a boy his own age with leprosy, and gave India the next thirty-four years
articles.deck: Graham Staines was fifteen, in Queensland, sitting through a missionary's slideshow. What he built in Baripada afterwards is still standing.

archiveMeta.editNote: The 2012 version of this piece was not original work and was withdrawn in August 2026. This is a new article, written from published reporting and reference sources listed at the foot, and focused on his work in Mayurbhanj.

body.v: This piece first ran in our July 2012 issue. That version has been withdrawn and the story researched and written again, with the focus on the work he did in Mayurbhanj across thirty-four years. Sources are listed at the end.
He was fifteen, sitting in a hall in Queensland while a visiting missionary showed photographs. One of them was of a boy in India called Josia Soren, about his own age, with severe leprosy.

Graham Staines could not explain afterwards why that particular picture would not leave him alone. Two years later, at a missions meeting, a speaker asked whether anyone in the room would go and work among people with leprosy. He said yes.
He arrived in India on his twenty-fourth birthday and stayed thirty-four years.
A boy in Palmwoods with a pen friend

He was born on 18 January 1941 in Palmwoods, on what is now Queensland's Sunshine Coast, the second child of William and Elizabeth Staines. He did well at school, then took a job in the office of a local garage and went to night classes to learn accountancy. He was heading for an ordinary and comfortable Australian working life.

In 1956 he began writing to a pen friend in India. Shantanu Satpathy lived in Baripada, the district town of Mayurbhanj in Orissa, and the two boys turned out to share a birthday. They wrote to each other about the plants and animals of their two countries. Long before he ever saw the place, Baripada was a real town to him with a real person in it.
That is worth pausing on. The photograph gave him the need. The letters gave him the address.
Three languages, and a song about polio

He went out in 1965 and joined the Evangelical Missionary Society of Mayurbhanj, which has a founding story that is not the one people expect. It was started in 1895 by Kate Allenby of the Queensland Baptist Missionary Society, at the invitation of Sriram Chandra Bhanj Deo, the Maharaja of Mayurbhanj, who had asked for it.

Staines learned Oriya, then Santhali, then Ho. He got good enough at Santhali that the local administration asked him to write a song in it to help publicise a polio immunisation drive. He wrote the song.

Years later he was still at it, handing out leaflets for the Pulse Polio campaign while Gladys drove the station wagon at the head of the awareness procession. He was president-designate of the Baripada Rotary club. None of that is mission work in the narrow sense. It is what happens when someone decides a town is theirs.
People knew the Australian on the bicycle in the sun hat. They called him Saibo.
The leprosy home

In 1982 he got the Mayurbhanj Leprosy Home registered as a society under Indian law, and in 1983 he took over running the mission. Those two administrative acts are the whole of his method: he made the thing legal, permanent and inspectable, and then he ran it.

The home housed and treated somewhere between seventy and a hundred people at a time. Leprosy in rural Orissa in the 1980s was not primarily a medical problem. It was a social one. A diagnosis meant being put out of your village, and the disease carried an untouchability that outlasted the cure by years.

So the work was not only bandaging. Patients whose disease had been arrested were taught to weave mats and baskets from sabai grass and tree leaves, so they had a trade to go back with. That mattered more than it sounds: a cured patient with no income was a cured patient who would be turned away twice, once for the disease and once for the begging.

When somebody recovered and still had nowhere on earth to go, Staines found them a place inside the compound. Ten families ended up living in the rehabilitation community. Two compounds, a farm, and around twenty-seven churches across the district had grown up around the work by the end.
He wanted more. His ambition was to build the centre into a full hospital, so that patients needing reconstructive surgery would not have to travel for it.
The dairy
The detail that says most about the work is the milk.

The mission ran a dairy farm, and its milk sold well in Baripada. Think about what that means. People who would not have shaken hands with a leprosy patient were buying milk from a farm attached to the leprosy home, and thinking nothing of it.
That is stigma being dismantled by ordinary commerce, and it does not happen by accident.

Somebody had to decide the farm was worth running, keep the quality up, and wait for the town to forget what it had once believed about the people living up the road. That is years of unremarkable decisions producing a result no campaign could have produced.
The night of the fire
A fire tore through Baripada and left around a hundred people dead and many more badly burned. The local hospital could not cope with the numbers.

Graham and Gladys spent the nights nursing the injured. He was a mission administrator with an accountancy background and she was a trained nurse, and when the town needed hands they were simply there, doing it, for as long as it took.
The Ho New Testament

The Ho are an indigenous people of eastern India, and their language had no complete New Testament. Staines worked as an editorial checker on the translation, going through the manuscript against the original text. It was published in 1997.

It is unglamorous work of the kind that lasts. A translation stays in use long after the person who proofread it is forgotten. He had a reputation as a compelling preacher, but the book is the object that outlived him.

Gladys Weatherhead had arrived in 1981, a trained nurse from Ipswich in Queensland who came out on a short youth mission and volunteered at the centre. They married in 1983 and lived in an old house in the mission compound. They had three children: Esther, Philip and Timothy.

On the night of 22 January 1999, Graham Staines and his two sons, Philip and Timothy, were killed at the village of Manoharpur when a mob set fire to the van they were sleeping in. Philip was ten. Timothy was six.
In the inquiry that followed, allegations that Staines had coerced anyone into changing religion were examined and found to be unsupported by evidence. Gladys has rejected them too.
What Gladys said
Gladys Staines gave evidence to the commission that inquired into the deaths of her husband and her two sons. This is from her affidavit:
It is far from my mind to punish the persons who were responsible for the death of my husband Graham and my two children. But it is my desire and hope that they would repent and would be reformed.
body.attr: Gladys Staines, affidavit to the commission of inquiry, 1999
body.highlight: It is far from my mind to punish

body.v: She did not leave. She stayed in Orissa and kept the leprosy work running for another five years, and went home to Queensland in 2004. In 2005 the Government of India gave her the Padma Shri. She still serves as honorary secretary of the mission society, from Townsville.
What is there now

A hostel for forty boys named after Philip and Timothy opened in 2003. A fifteen-bed hospital named after Graham opened in 2004, which is the hospital he had wanted, finished after he was gone. A girls' care centre named after Kate Allenby, who started the mission back in 1895, opened in 2013.

None of it has been smooth. The hospital suspended its activity in 2019 after a dispute with the state government. This is not a story that resolves neatly, and it would be dishonest to write it as though it does.
Every January, around fifty Christian families at Manoharpur gather outside the small church there to pray and remember. They still call him Saibo.
So what, in 2026?

Almost nothing he did would work as content. He learned three languages, which took years and produced no visible milestone. He filed the paperwork to register a leprosy home as a society, which is the least shareable act imaginable and is also the reason the place survived him. He proofread a New Testament in a language most Indians have never heard spoken. He sold milk until people stopped flinching.
There is no moment in any of that. There is no before-and-after. It is thirty-four years of turning up in the same town.

If you are seventeen and wondering what a life spent on something actually looks like, it looks less like a decision and more like an address. One photograph, one pen friend, one town you keep going back to until you know its languages. He was fifteen when he saw the picture. He was twenty-four when he arrived. In between, he learned accountancy and waited.

Sources: Philip Malayil, “Staines, Graham”, Dictionary of Christian Biography in Asia; Ruben Banerjee's contemporaneous reporting for India Today, February 1999; Sampad Patnaik, Indian Express, 23 January 2019, on the hospital's suspension; Debabrata Mohanty, Hindustan Times, 24 January 2024; the report of the commission of inquiry, including Gladys Staines's affidavit.
